sentence: Dapagliflozin is a type of medicine known as a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor.
note: NHS says it is an SGLT2 inhibitor; the full name is the standard expansion of the abbreviation.

sentence: In type 2 diabetes the NHS says it makes the kidneys remove extra sugar from the body in the urine, which lowers blood sugar.
note: NHS: increases the amount of sugar removed from the body when you pee.

sentence: It can also reduce the amount of work the heart needs to do to pump blood around the body.
In chronic kidney disease the NHS says it works by reducing pressure and swelling (inflammation) in the kidneys.
The NHS says it starts to work after about 2 hours to reduce blood glucose levels, but it may take up to a week to take full effect.
The NHS lists thrush, back pain and passing urine more often than usual as common side effects
Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) can happen when dapagliflozin is taken with other diabetes medicines, including insulin or a sulfonylurea such as gliclazide, and can cause dizziness or shakiness
note: NHS names insulin/sulfonylureas like gliclazide; dizzy or shaky; Diabetes UK agrees.

sentence: Feeling sleepy or dizzy can occur, and the NHS says driving, cycling or using tools or machines is best avoided until these symptoms pass

note: NHS lists symptoms; Leeds describes ketone build-up (DKA); NHS England leaflet says call doctor or NHS 111. 999 per site rule.

sentence: Dapagliflozin is a tablet that the NHS says is available only with a prescription.
The NHS says it is mainly used to treat type 2 diabetes, usually when metformin cannot be taken or when the current medicine is not controlling blood sugar well.
Diabetes UK says it can be taken alone or with metformin, a DPP-4 inhibitor, a sulphonylurea or insulin.
It is also used for heart failure and chronic kidney disease.
In heart failure the NHS says it can reduce the risk of the heart getting weaker and help symptoms such as tiredness.
In chronic kidney disease it helps to slow the rate at which the condition gets worse.

NICE recommends it as an add-on to standard care for symptomatic chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction in adults, and for symptomatic chronic heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction.
NICE also recommends it for chronic kidney disease in adults who meet the criteria in its guidance.
note: TA775 limits the recommendation to adults meeting set criteria.
